It means that we are, for the first time, able to begin to pair human biological ingenuity with machine pattern recognition at scale. And we are only at the beginning. The implications stretch beyond medicine. Protein engineering touches everything from clean energy enzymes to biodegradable materials to carbon capture molecules. When we begin to treat biology not just as a mystery but as code (information) that can be read, predicted, and rewritten, life on the other side of that foggy bridge begins to look very different from the past. This is not science fiction. This is happening now. We are standing at the edge of a new kind of discovery—one that transcends disciplines, fuses insights, and opens doors we didn’t know existed. Michael Levin and Intelligence at the Cellular Level Imagine a robot smaller than a grain of sand built entirely from your own cells. It needs no batteries. No programming. No external commands. You place it near damaged tissue in your brain, and it moves—on its own—to the wound site. It parks itself there. And over the next three days, the neurons beneath it begin to knit themselves back together. The damage heals. The robot, having completed its work, quietly dissolves back into the body it came from. This sounds like medicine from the year 2200. But it has already happened in a laboratory at Tufts University. 121 To understand how, we need to rethink something fundamental about our own biology. Remember protein folding—how amino acids twist and contort into the precise shapes that make life possible. But proteins don’t assemble themselves into organs. Cells do that. Every organ in your body was built by cells. Your heart didn’t arrive preassembled. Cells constructed it—coordinating across millions of individual units to form chambers, valves, and electrical pathways that would beat three billion times over a lifetime. The same is true of your lungs, your liver, your eyes. And your brain. The roughly eighty-six billion neurons that give rise to your thoughts, your memories, your sense of self—all of it was built, piece by piece, by cells that somehow knew what to do. We don’t usually think of cells this way. We think of them as building blocks, passive material. But they’re not the bricks. They’re the bricklayers. Which raises a question: If cells can do all that, are they intelligent? This is the question that has consumed Michael Levin, a developmental biologist at Tufts, for decades. 122 Not just whether cells have some form of intelligence—but how far down the ladder of complexity intelligence actually goes. At what point do goal-directed behavior, problem-solving, and agency first appear? Only in brains? In nervous systems? Or do they reach further down—into individual cells? Every cell in your body, Levin argues, descended from organisms that once lived independently—single-celled creatures that had to navigate, decide, and survive on their own. 123 When those cells came together to form bodies, they didn’t lose that competence. They networked it. Your heart cells coordinate without asking your brain for permission. Your gut makes decisions your conscious mind never sees. The brain, in this view, isn’t the origin of biological intelligence. It’s the most sophisticated expression of a principle that runs far deeper—a principle encoded in the electrical conversations between cells in the way tissues solve problems and pursue goals. So how did Levin build that tiny healing robot? In 2023, his team created what they call anthrobots—tiny biological machines assembled from human tracheal cells. 124 The cells are covered in hairlike projections called cilia, which normally help clear mucus from your airways. But when Levin’s team removed these cells from their usual context and let them self-assemble in a dish, something unexpected happened. The cells organized themselves into spherical structures and began to move. Some traveled in straight lines. Some spiraled. Some clustered together into larger superbots . No one programmed them to do this. No one edited their DNA. The cells simply … did it. Then came the real surprise. When researchers placed these anthrobots near a scratch wound in a layer of neurons, the bots migrated to the damage, settled across the gap, and somehow encouraged the nerve cells to regrow. “These bots can move across a damaged site, sit there, and actually help the nerves knit across,” said Gizem Gumuskaya, who led the research in Levin’s lab. 125 The mechanism isn’t fully understood—it’s not merely mechanical pressure, because inert materials don’t produce the same effect. The anthrobots are doing something active. Something that looks, from the outside, like purpose. The implications for medicine are profound. Today, if you lose a limb, it’s gone. We can fit you with a prosthetic—remarkable engineering—but we cannot regrow what was lost. Now imagine a future where we simply communicate with the cellular intelligence that built that limb in the first place and ask it to build another. This isn’t science fiction. Levin’s team has already induced limb regeneration in frogs that normally cannot regenerate. His anthrobots are being explored for clearing arterial plaque, repairing spinal cord injuries, even targeting cancer cells—all using the patient’s own tissue, requiring no immunosuppression, leaving no permanent implant behind. You can begin to imagine a future where some of what we think of today as sophisticated medicine will look crude and mechanical. A world where high school biology classes teach our kids about how we use the same cellular intelligence that built our body in the first place to repair it when it gets damaged. Just using information and cellular agency or intelligence. Two decades before Gumuskaya placed those first anthrobots near wounded neurons, Ray Kurzweil described almost exactly this scenario.
